title: Small area estimation using R, with application to poverty mapping
abstract: Small area estimation is a promising, but also well established and well developed family of methods to gain insights on detailed domains or areas. Not widely used in statistical offices yet, available resources in R provide an opportunity to change that. Existing R packages designed for small area estimation with a special focus on the applicability for poverty mapping are reviewed. Applications to poverty mapping are presented to illustrate some of the available functions.

title: Distances with mixed-type variables, some proposals
abstract: Nearest-neighbor methods have become popular in official statistics, mainly because of their use in imputation problems (cf. Andridge and Little, 2010) or statistical matching (cf. D’Orazio et al, 2006). They also play a key role in machine learning, where a high number of variants have been proposed (cf. Hastie et al, 2009). Key decisions in nearest-neighbor methods concern: (i) the variables to include (when many potential candidate exist) and, (ii) the distance function to apply. The first decision depends on the scope of the application (see D’Orazio et al., 2019, for statistical matching applications) and will not be the tackled here. The choice of the distance function depends mainly on the type of the variables selected in step (i). When all the variables are of the same type, i.e. all numerical or all categorical, many options exist (distances for categorical variables use differently the corresponding dummy variables). Unfortunately, relatively few options are available in the presence of mixed-type variables. The most popular distance for mixed-type variables is the Gower’s one, implemented in several functions/packages in R (see e.g. van der Loo, 2019). It can be viewed as an average of the distances calculated variable by variable, whereas the single distances are all scaled to range from 0 (both the units present the same value) to 1 (max distance). The Gower distance is appealing because allows for missing values and permits to introduce a user-defined weighting scheme when averaging distances over the single variables. The discussion on the weighting schemes in Gower’s distance is sometimes misleading since it often ignores that that the unweighted “standard” version tends to favor categorical rather than numeric variables. In fact, the maximum distance (value 1) is observed more frequently on a categorical variable rather than on a numeric one where the city-block (Manhattan) distance, scaled with the range, is considered. In addition, the latter distance is sensitive to the presence of outliers. This work try to address the main drawbacks that affect the calculation of the overall unweighted Gower’s distance by suggesting some modifications. Simple modifications try to attenuate the impact of outliers on the scaled city-block distance; more effective modifications seem those derived by the kernel density estimation methods. The work will also compare the proposed approaches with some alternative distances for mixed-type variables that are available in R. The results of some experiments related to imputation through nearest neighbor distance hotdeck based on “standard” and modified Gower’s distance will be presented.

title: emdi 2.0.0: A Framework for Producing Estimates based on Area-Level Models in R
abstract: The R package emdi facilitates the estimation of regionally disaggregated indicators using small area methods and includes tools for processing, assessing, and presenting the results. The current package mainly includes unit-level small area models, in particular the empirical best predictor (Molina and Rao, 2010). However, access to unit-level data like census, administrative or register data is challenging because of confidentiality constraints. In contrast, area-level models are less demanding with respect to a) data requirements as only aggregates of auxiliary variables are needed for estimating regional indicators and b) computational resources. In addition, design-based properties of area-level models can be achieved due to incorporating survey weights. Therefore, the area-level model (Fay and Herriot, 1979) and various extensions have been added to a new version of the package emdi. These extensions include amongst others a) adjusted variance estimation methods for the random effects (Li and Lahiri, 2010; Yoshimori and Lahiri, 2014), b) log and arcsin transformation for the dependent variable with corresponding back transformations (Slud and Maiti, 2006), c) spatial and robust Fay-Herriot models (Pratesi and Salvati, 2008; Warnholz, 2016), and d) Fay-Herriot models when the auxiliary variables are measured with an error (Ybarra and Lohr, 2008). Depending on the particular area-level model analytical, bootstrap and jackknife MSE estimation methods are implemented. User-friendly tools like a stepwise variable selection function, model diagnostics, benchmarking options, high quality maps and export of the results to Excel enable the user a complete analysis procedure, from model building to inference. The functionality of the package is demonstrated by illustrative examples based on synthetic EU-SILC data for Austrian districts.

title: R package SamplingStrata: new developments and extension to Spatial Sampling
abstract: The R package SamplingStrata was developed in 2011 as an instrument to optimize the design of stratified samples. Since then, it has been used in official statistical production processes not only by a number of National Statistical Institutes, but also by important organisations as World Bank, Eurostat, Bank of Italy. The optimization is performed by considering the stratification variables available in the sampling frame, and the precision constraints on target estimates of the survey (Ballin & Barcaroli, 2014). The genetic algorithm at the basis of the optimization step explores the universe of the possible alternative stratifications determining for each of them the best allocation, that is the one of minimum total size that allows to satisfy the precision constraints: the final optimal solution is the one that ensures the global minimum sample size. One fundamental requirement to make this approach feasible is the possibility to estimate the variability of target variables in generated strata; in general, as target variable values are not available in the frame, but only proxy ones, anticipated variance is calculated by modelling the relations between target and proxy variables. New functions have been implemented in order to correctly calculate the anticipated variance, in particular taking into account heteroscedasticity of residuals. In case of spatial sampling, it is important to consider not only the total model variance, but also the co-variance derived by the spatial auto-correlation. The last release of SamplingStrata enables to consider both components of variance, including spatial auto-correlation, in order to obtain more efficient samples.

title: mquantreg: An R package for estimating generalized linear M-quantile regression models
abstract: The R package mquantreg enables regression estimation, diagnostics and testing for generalized linear M-quantile models. This type of robust regression using influence functions is suitable for many applications. It is based on the Huber estimator utilizing a tuning constant, which controls the degree of robustification of the regression results in the presence of outliers. Therefore, these models bridge between quantile and expectile regression, examining the whole conditional distribution of the data. The mquantreg package includes different models contingent on the type of the dependent variable. It comprises a) continuous (Breckling and Chambers, 1988), b) binomial (Chambers et al., 2016) and c) count data versions (poisson (Tzavidis et al., 2015), quasi-poisson, negative binomial (Chambers et al., 2014)). The estimation for the binary and count data models is a generalization of the robust quasi-likelihood approach of Cantoni and Ronchetti (2001). The continuous model can be estimated using maximum likelihood (Bianchi et al., 2018), under which likelihood ratio-type and Wald test statistics can be used to test linear hypotheses about the regression coefficients. Additionally, a goodness-of-fit measure as an analogue to R2 in ordinary least squares estimation has been implemented. Since M-quantile regression is not scale equivariant, different proposals for nuisance scale parameters like the estimator proposed by Chambers and Tzavidis (2006), as well as the corrected version of Dawber (2017) are provided. Furthermore, the estimation of q-scores (Kokic et al., 1997) is set up for all model types and user-friendly tools like model selection based on q-scores (Dawber, 2017), as well as diagnostic plots are included.

title: Spatial Spread Sampling Using Weakly Associated Vectors
abstract: Geographical data are generally autocorrelated. In this case, it is preferable to select spread units. In this paper, we propose a new method for selecting well-spread samples from a finite spatial population with equal or unequal inclusion probabilities. The proposed method is based on the definition of a spatial structure by using a stratification matrix. Our method exactly satisfies given inclusion probabilities and provides samples that are very well-spread. A set of simulations shows that our method outperforms other existing methods such as the Generalized Random Tessellation Stratified (GRTS) or the Local Pivotal Method (LPM). Analysis of the variance on a real dataset shows that our method is more accurate than these two. Furthermore, a variance estimator is proposed. The proposed method is implemented in the R package “WaveSampling”.

title: Classy classifications in R
abstract: The use of standard classifications is important within statistical bureaus. It infiltrates virtually all aspects of statistical production, from specifying needs through to dissemination. Diverging from standards may contribute to problems within a statistical production, difficulties in comparisons between time periods and inconsistencies between various statistical outputs. It can be time consuming for individuals within the organisation to create their own, ad hoc solutions, and frustrating when users are forced to move between several applications and data forms to retrieve the information they require. In this paper, I outline Statistics Norway’s solution to maintaining standard classifications and present a new, easy way to access these standards with an R package klassR. This package has functions for searching, retrieving and applying standards using Statistics Norway’s API. This provides the user with all the necessary tools to use the standards, all from within the R environment. This easy access can save time for the users and increase the use of standards, increasing consistencies within and among statistical outputs.

title: Methods for classifying nonprofit organizations according to their field of activity: A report on semi-automated methods based on text
abstract: Nonprofit organizations (NPOs) play a crucial role in modern societies (Anheier & Seibel, 2013; Evers & Laville, 2004). However, most national statistical offices barely keep track of this sector, and have not implemented a Satellite account on NPOs as recommended by the UN Statistics Division yet (United Nations, 2018). One central piece of information concerns NPOs’ fields of activity. Many available data sets do not contain such information in readily usable form, because classification by fields of activity is missing or of poor quality (see, for example, Grønbjerg & Paarlberg, 2002:588 on consistency problems with NTEE classifications in IRS data in the U.S.). In trying to tackle this common problem, we have implemented two semi-automated methods based on textual data in R: rule-based classification, and machine-learning with curated keywords (Zhai & Massung, 2016:300-302). We use those methods to classify all Austrian associations (~80.000) based on the International Classification of Nonprofit Organizations (ICNPO) (Salamon & Anheier, 1992; United Nations, 2018). Those methods can provide a solution when quantitative data on the activities of NPOs are needed but neither readily available from administrative data, nor accessible through additional sources with high information content (long high-quality mission statements, tax records etc.). We find that in such a setting, rule-based classification based on only the organizations’ names performs well in terms of precision and sensitivity. Hence, we share our insights on how to efficiently implement such a rule-based approach in R. We also share open-source sample code that is free to use and adapt.

title: Selective editing of categorical variables with random forests: results of the implementation in the statistical production
abstract: Selective editing, as part of the statistical data editing strategies (EDIMBUS, GSDEM), plays an important role to identify influential errors in the datasets. In 2013, Statistics Spain (INE) proposed an optimization-based approach modeling measurement errors applied on continuous variables that has been used in the editing strategies of some Short-Term Business Statistics during the last six years. Here, we present the application of a random forest model for the measurement error of categorical variables. The main goal of this model is to classify influential errors based on both observed variable values and on auxiliary information. This proposal paves the way to use other statistical learning algorithms (SVM, neural networks, etc.) to automate the editing tasks upon the basis of already existing information about the process. The software implementation of this methodology has been done in an R package called categObsPredModelParam, which is part of a whole ecosystem of R packages internally used in Statistics Spain (INE) implementing a modular approach to the standardization of the statistical production process and strongly focused on a key-value pair data representation. We present the performance of this technique both in simulation studies and with the results of the implementation in the production of the Spanish edition of the European Health Survey. We share the encouraging results in the simulations (AUC around 0.80) and lessons learnt from the implementation in real production conditions.

title: Balanced Imputation for Swiss Cheese Nonresponse
abstract: Swiss cheese nonresponse, also known as non-monotone nonresponse, occurs when all variables of a survey contain missing values without a particular pattern. The estimators of the parameters of interest can be significantly affected by the missing values, which leads to a bias and an increased variability. To reduce the effects of nonresponse, the missing values are usually imputed. When several variables of a dataset need to be imputed, it may be difficult to preserve the distributions and the relations between the variables. A new method using random imputations by donors will be presented. It extends the balanced K-nearest neighbor imputation to the treatment of Swiss cheese nonresponse. The construction of the method meets the following requirements. First, a nonrespondent should be imputed by neighboring donors. Next, the same donor should impute all the missing values of the same nonrespondent. Finally, donors are selected to meet balancing constraints to eliminate the variance due to random imputation. To meet all the requirements, a matrix of imputation probabilities is constructed using calibration techniques. The donors are then selected with these imputation probabilities and balanced sampling methods. The method will be implemented in the ‘SwissCheese’ R package.

title: sdcLog:1 Utilities for Statistical Disclosure Control in the Context of Research Data Centres
abstract: Research Data Centres (RDC’s) often provide access to micro data only within “secure environments” at their premises. Users working there with confidential data cannot export their results out of the secure environment by themselves. Thus, the RDC’s staff members need to check the results for potential disclosure risk before forwarding them out of the secure environment. Users have to make sure that all confidentiality requirements are met. This needs to be documented in a log file. As this can become cumbersome, the R package sdcLog provides a handful of functions that make it easy for users to show that their results meet all confidentiality requirements. “Results” in this context means descriptive statistics, graphics, and models. sdcLog aims to provide a simple interface (leveraging S3 methods) to lower the burden for users as much as possible. Simultaneously, the package makes it easy for RDC staff to confirm whether all requirements are fulfilled.

title: riot: R Input-Output Tools
abstract: The R package riot1 contains functions that are helpful when dealing with supply and use matrices and constructing input-output tables. The functions described in the following are often computationally intensive. Thus I implemented them using Rcpp2 to achieve a higher computational efficiency. The package includes an implementation of the GRAS algorithm (described in Junius and Oosterhaven (2003) and Temurshoev, Miller, and Bouwmeester (2013)), that can be used for balancing (or updating) matrices to new row and column sums. In the construction process of (multi country) input-output tables, efficient and easy handling of supply and use is very important. To this end, I created a SUT object class in R’s object system R63. The SUT class bundles the supply and (import and domestic) use matrices in one object and additionally provides methods to 1) check the consistency of the supply and use system, 2) aggregate to a different industry/product classification, 3) update (benchmark) supply and use tables to new data using the SUTRAS algorithm from Temurshoev and Timmer (2011) and 4) calculate an input-output table from it (using the recommended types of calculation as in Beutel (2008)) Finally, there are also functions that help in the analysis of input-output tables, such as the random walk centrality from Blöchl et al. (2011).
affiliations: The Vienna Institute for International Economic Studies

title: Classifying the Country of Birth using Supervised Learning
abstract: German migration statistics face user demands to report the country of birth. At the same time, responding registration offices do not fully report the information. Hence the item country of birth has quality issues. However the respondents collect and report information on the place of birth in a text field. In recent years, the information on the country of birth was extracted from the birthplace information using an automatic approach based on an internal repertory of localities. This approach has accuracy limitations and does not allow a complete imputation of missing values. We present an approach to classify the country of birth from the text information on the place of birth using supervised learning hence maximizing coverage while minimizing clerical efforts. We will furthermore address critical issues for putting such methods into practice.

title: Unstructured text as a source of information
abstract: In the age of big data, one of our main challenges is that much information is available only in an unstructured fashion. Examples include reports, notes, applications, web pages and summaries. Archives, moreover, are filled with information that is unstructured. Annual reports are one type of unstructured text that contain a lot of potentially useful information to aid survey data, build registers and develop indicators. We present a solution to parse complex text data. The idea is to structure the unstructured textual information found in annual reports. These reports are available in a picture format, and the solution will demonstrate how to read the annual reports into R with OCR to extract the text, structure the information using regex and the stringr-package, and organizing the information in a Shiny-app. We also suggest how this could be used to enhance and build statistical indicators.

title: Functional data analysis in Bayes Spaces with an Application to spatio-temporal population data
abstract: Probability density functions are frequently used to characterize the distributional properties of large-scale database systems. As functional compositions, densities carry primarily relative information. As such, standard methods of functional data analysis (FDA) are not appropriate for their statistical processing and thus a compositional alternative is proposed. The aim of this presentation is to outline a concise methodology for functional principal component analysis of densities based on the geometry of the Bayes space B2 of functional compositions. Advances of the proposed approach are demonstrated using a real-world example of population pyramids in Upper Austria. For compositional analysis we also introduce the R package robCompositions.

title: Revisiting Rogers and Castros’ multi-exponential model migration schedules
abstract: The decision to establish a fixed initial value in the optimizations of multi-exponential migration models (Rogers and Castro, 1981) has long been the one that has been imposed. However, to pose mathematically the ignorance of the parameters by means of a uniform distribution offers us the opportunity to simulate the initial values and see what happens if we open this black box. The use of this kind of models has a paramount importance when population is projected and smoothing must be done besides to have an equation to replicate the model for analysis and comparisons. This paper look at the optimization of model parameters when they are applied to an international migration case, changing the fixed initial values for the simulations of uniform distributions. The aim is to abstract the total ignorance of the distribution of each one of them. The sources of information are summarized in those provided by the censuses of twelve countries in Latin America on the place of residence 5 years ago. The results include the application of the optimization with the incorporation of the change of the initial values, and shows how the location parameters μ2 and μ3 are not significant in the estimation of the Mean Square Error (ECM) for some cases, which means that the theoretical assumptions may not be followed. The second part of the analysis, the tool created to talk about the set of country-to-country migrations mostly characterized by the presence of working age population using the package Rilostat to obtain the data This work theoretically contributes to the assumptions when using the models of Rogers and Castro (1981), as well as a prototype package migraR for free replication that can be downloaded from Github while the work is done to uploaded to CRAN.
affiliations: Autonomous University of Barcelona; International Labour Organization

title: A Sparse Matrix Tool in R for Multidimensional Hierarchical Aggregation
abstract: Commonly, tabular aggregations involve hierarchical classifications (hierarchies) that follow a tree structure. Free hierarchies are more advanced. Then, each code can be specified as a formula involving other codes. Addition or union is specified by the plus sign and subtraction or compliment is specified by the minus sign. Statistics Norway’s modernized calculations of municipal accounts involve complicated free hierarchies. The intention was to do the computations by an implementation of the Validation and Transformation Language (VTL), but this approach turned out to be too inefficient. Instead, a general hierarchical computing method was implemented in R as the function HierarchyCompute in the package SSBtools. Hierarchies and crossed hierarchies are represented by sparse matrices according to the Matrix package. The aggregates are obtained by matrix multiplication. The matrix representation therefore makes it easy to see how each output code is calculated from the input codes. A spin-off from the general implementation is that hierarchy specifications, usual in statistical disclosure control software, can be managed. This has been utilized in the package SmallCountRounding, which can be used to protect frequency tables.

title: Analysis of trajectories into retirement using the Danish labour market registry
abstract: The Danish labour market registry is a longitudinal registry containing the labour market status of all individuals residing in Denmark. Apart from registering when and for how long and individual is employed or unemployed, the registry indicates whether an individual is retired, studying, or receiving some type of benefits (e.g. pregnancy leave). Sequence analysis and joint models for longitudinal and survival data are two methods for analyzing longitudinal data such as those from the labour market registry. We show the use of these two methods in R using an example on early retirement pension. To be more precise we investigate the effect of a policy change in the age of eligibility for early retirement on the relation between labour market status and retirement timing in three cohorts.

title: Automation in calculation and presentation of educational indicators
abstract: In this presentation we cover the automated process for generation of education indicators for a published, official database (https://indikatoren.bifie.at/; available in Spring 2020). This includes the following steps: 1. Calculating correct estimates and standard errors for national or international Large Scale Assessments of students achievement by the means of BIFIEsurvey (on CRAN). Considerations of anonymity, eg. checking for small sample sizes and distinct outcome patterns, play a heavy role in this step too. 2. Automated generation of tables of coefficients by the means of openxlsx (on CRAN). Tables are enriched with methodological and statistical remarks as well as good-looking layout. 3. Automated generation of graphs in scalable vector format (SVG). For this, we created our own tool (svgtools) that is in preparation for publication on CRAN. It allows us to produce graphs from a small set of templates (designed in Adobe Illustrator) that fully correspond to the corporate design.

session: R in the Organization and in Production
title: DevOps and R: Experiences at Statistics Austria
abstract: In this contribution we present and outline the steps we have taken to facilitate the automated building and deployment of R packages for internal usage at Statistics Austria. We discuss our environment that consists of an R server (Rstudio-Server Pro), a git-server (Bitbucket), a build-server (Jenkins) and an artifact repository manager (JFrog Artifactory). In order to connect these servers, we developed a (complex) pipeline template and an internal utility package (useSTAT) which helps users to consistently set up R-based projects and linking those projects to a git-repository or a continuous integration process. We discuss the reasons for this setup and identify strengths and weaknesses of this approach. Furthermore, we show a typical use case and illustrate why we want to formalize our setup even more in the future to ensure consistent quality checks for all our internal R packages.

session: R in the Organization and in Production
title: The awesome list of official statistics software: 100 … and counting
abstract: The exchange and reuse of statistical software among statistical institutes has proven to be valuable for many years. In domains such as statistical disclosure control, SDMX and statistical dissemination there were always a few well-known solutions that were used by many offices. The software landscape was relatively clear. These days this landscape is much more complex and dynamic. There are numerous packages for statistical methods which are continuously improved. This makes it much harder to maintain an overview of what is there and what to use in what case. Hence there is a clear need to support the knowledge about the existence and use of generic official statistics software. In particular this is the case for open source tools that can be accessed and installed easily in another environment, such as R packages. A popular way of exchanging such information is a so called awesome list [1]. In 2017 the authors of this abstract started the so called awesome list of official statistics software [2] which recently reached a milestone of 100 entries. In this talk we want to motivate even more participants of uRos2020 to share their work with a wider audience with the help of the awesome list and keep the growth going. An awesome list is a community approach to knowledge management. People can help improve the list by adding change requests that conform to the contribution guidelines. The growth of the list is therefore a collective success. At the start of the list it contained those software packages known to the initiators. Contribution guidelines were formulated, such as the requirement that the software is used in the production of official statistics by at least one institute. This was added to guarantee some matureness of the packages. Another guideline is that item links to some place where the software is downloadable, encouraging an easy installation process. To give the user an indication of its use, the list is organised according to the Generic Statistical Business Process Model (GSBPM). Figure 1 shows some GSBPM statistics on the current contents of the list.

session: R in the Organization and in Production
title: From Airflow to Docker - R in an Open Source Production Environment
abstract: The KOF Swiss Economic Institute at ETH Zurich (Switzerland) surveys more than 10K companies on a regular basis, creates economic indicators and forecasts as it monitors the national economy. Today, KOF updates its website in automated fashion and operates automated data pipelines to partners such as regional statistical offices or the Swiss National Bank. KOF has migrated its production to a license cost free open source environment that is powerful yet light weight and easy to maintain. This talk shows that R does not only fit into KOF's production environment but plays a crucial role in bringing parts of the system together and fosters developing that environment further. For example, R packages are automatically checked, built and uploaded to a self-hosted, internal R archive network in order to foster deployment and manage package versions. At KOF, R has been used in production since 2011.

session: R in the Organization and in Production
title: Persephone: Process-oriented facilitator for RJDemetra including support of hierarchical time series
abstract: Seasonal Adjustment (SA) is one of the key processes especially when producing time series for estimates in economic statistics. In this regard the R-package persephone is developed to enable easy processing during the production of seasonally adjusted estimates. It builds on top of the well-known package RJDemetra and provides analytical visualization tools such as interactive plots to support the SA expert. The package incorporates facilities to easily assess the quality of the seasonal adjustment through personalized dashboards containing selected plots and diagnostics. Furthermore it supports hierarchical time series and tackles the issue of quality assessment of direct vs indirect adjustment. The paper describes the functionality of the R package and shows examples to demonstrate how persephone could be used to assess the quality of hierarchical time series.

session: R in the Organization and in Production
title: Automation of the Quarterly National Accounts compilation process
abstract: The process of quarterly national accounts (QNA) compilation includes many repetitive tasks each quarter. Indeed, most of these tasks can be automated to save more time which can be in favor of other tasks of economic analysis and synthesis. To do this, the taskscheduleR package for windows users, allows the QNA division to automate the execution of R scripts related to the common workflow that load data from the web and other sources, then perform data processing and manipulation before creating reports and visualizations, after that we can schedule econometric tasks and finally export the outputs to convenient format. This work process automation can be interrupted by sending alerts to the responsible if an error is observed or for other programmed reasons. The objective of this work is to demonstrate the powerful and beneficial use of the automation process to compile the QNA using R.

session: R for web and other data
title: Using R for Web Data Collection at Scale
abstract: Over the last decade the internet has become a prominent source of information for everyone. While the internet is not without challenges when used as a source of data its omnipresence in everyday live, industry, social activity, tourism, commerce and many-many more areas opens the door to a myriad of possible applications some of them yet unthought of. In this talk will cover R’s suitability to do internet data collection also known as web scraping at scale and in production: i.e. in an automated, robust, and repeated fashion aimed to be integrated into a broader data gathering, data processing or data analytics pipeline. The talk will sketch out how R can be used together with other big data technologies and will also provide a discussion about its suitability and experiences made using it for collecting thousands of website each day.

session: R for web and other data
title: R for Web scraping Online Job Adverts and computing potential indicators
abstract: In this paper we describe our experience in using R for collecting data regarding job vacancies from the online environment and for computing some new potential indicators using these data sets. After testing several web-scraping techniques, we chose the RSelenium package because it allowed us an easy automation of the data collection process. Data were collected during 1 year from several Romanian job advertising Web sites and National Employment Agency and after a cleaning and preprocessing step were used to compute potentially new indicators for labor force statistics. The specific characteristics of this data collection process allowed us to propose and compute statistical indicators with a frequency higher than the classical job vacancies survey. All steps, starting from data collection to the final estimates were implemented using different R packages. We also show the difficulties encountered during this process and the lessons learned.
affiliations: University of Bucharest and National Institute of Statistics Romania; National Institute of Statistics Romania and Ecological University of Bucharest; Ecological University of Bucharest and National Institute of Statistics Romania; The Bucharest University of Economic Studies and National Institute of Statistics Romania; National Institute of Statistics Romania

session: R for web and other data
title: Between R and Excel - The ETER Data Validation and Quality Process
abstract: R is the tool of choice in a project called ETER1 (European Tertiary Education Register), contracted by the European Commission. ETER is a database collecting information on the level of European higher education institutions. Within the project, data for nearly 3,000 higher education institutions per year have been collected for 6 years (the academic years 2011/2012 until 2016/2017). In total, the dataset currently contains 17,285 rows and 618 columns of data. R is used in the project for data analysis as well as the data validation and data quality process. The sheer amount of data combined with the implementation of a standardized data collection in 37 different – and very heterogeneous – countries proved to be a challenging task regarding data quality. Therefore, a multi-level data management process has been chosen in order to find typos, logical inconsistencies, missing values, outliers etc. and ensure a high data quality. R plays – together with Excel – a vital role in this process (see step 4). First, R is used in the data validation process, where the data are checked on completeness, accuracy (e.g. formats) and consistency (e.g. sums). The outputs of this part of the project are data validation reports for each year and country. These reports are released by country experts only when all problems detected in the reports are solved or at least flagged. Second, the whole data quality process is implemented within R. This process includes multiannual checks in order to detect (too) large differences between years, outliers, completeness indicators and country totals. The output of the data quality process is an MS-Excel file, which includes all notable cases (i.e. higher education institutions and variables per year) and complementary information (e.g. legal status, institution category, foundation year, etc.) in order to examine and flag these cases.

session: R for web and other data
title: A Web Service for Processing GPS Data from Mobile Phones
abstract: The transport unit of Statistics Austria has recently developed a mobile phone app for collecting data on goods transport by Austrian haulers. If the user chooses to enable GPS tracking, parts of the required information are determined automatically by a web service that we implemented in R. The service operates in three steps: First, the GPS data is validated and cleaned in an automated preprocessing step. Second, the preprocessed data is submitted to an external OSRM based routing service to calculate the fastest route on the road network. Third, the response from the service is parsed and processed to derive travel distance, transit countries, and border crossings. To facilitate communication between the service and the backend application of the mobile app, we set up a RESTful API with plumber that we deployed via rsconnect. This approach enabled us to decouple the development cycle of the service from that of the mobile application. Another advantage was that we could reuse existing R packages that were already operational inside the transport unit. For example, the web service uses the same routing backend that was originally set up for calculating distance matrices for the European road freight transport statistics. This way we were able to create a reliable and easily maintainable service while also preserving developer ressources.

session: R for web and other data
title: A set of R packages to compute population count from mobile network data
affiliations: Statistics Romania; University of Bucharest; Statistics Spain (INE)

session: R for web and other data
title: Geolocation of mobile devices with Hidden Markov Models
abstract: The incorporation of mobile network data into the standard production of official statistics in the European Statistical System (ESS) is taking a diversity of parallel initiatives ranging from tackling legal, ethical, business, and technological issues about the access/use of this data source to the development of novel statistical methodology to process this data. Both in the past and in the ongoing editions of the ESS project ESSnet on Big Data, together with activities by Eurostat and the ESS Task Force on Big Data and Trusted Smart Statistics, a modular approach named the ESS Reference Methodological Framework for Mobile Network Data has been under construction during the past months. One of the key modules in this production framework is the geolocation estimation of the events detected in the telecommunication network to produce population counts (present population, inbound tourists, domestic tourists, commuters, etc.). We present a methodological framework for the geolocation of mobile devices using hidden Markov models (HMMs). This framework provides probability distributions for the location of each device over a reference grid under many diverse circumstances depending on data availability. Once the mathematical description of the state of each device is specified, the core of these models is the computation of both the emission probabilities and the transition probabilities, which is undertaken depending on data availability thus allowing the user to adapt the framework to her particular case. Once the model is fitted, we apply the forward-backward algorithm to output the probability distribution for the location of each device over the reference grid, which will be the basis for the upper-level statistical computations in different statistical domains. This methodology has been implemented in an R package called destim developed in the aforementioned ESS project. We illustrate the use of this package with synthetic data produced by a mobile network data simulator also developed in the project.
affiliations: Statistics Spain; National Institute of Statistics Romania

title: timeseriesdb - Manage, Archive and Version Time Series with R and PostgreSQL
abstract: Data revisions are common in Official Statistics which results in idiosyncratic needs when managing and archiving data. This lightning talk introduces the all new version 1.0 of the {timeseriesdb} R package which was tailored to handle time series in Official Statistics: The package allows to store multiple versions (vintages) of the same time series, manages comprehensive, multi-lingual data descriptions and allows for fine grained access control through row level security (RLS). {timeseriesdb} uses the world's most advanced, relational open source database, PostgreSQL, as a data store and maps PostgreSQL relations to R time series representations. Thanks to its common, open source components, {timeseriesdb} is easy to install and maintain while offering substantial advantages over spreadsheets or other file based formats -- in particular when collaboratively working with data.

title: Estimating The Disaggregated Regional Official Statistics in Indonesia using EBLUP Benchmark-Small Area Estimation Method
abstract: The Empirical Best Linear Unbiased Prediction (EBLUP) method is a popular method in Small Area Estimation (SAE), but the estimated values cannot guarantee consistency with the estimated value of the area above it. Official statistics require consistency of estimated aggregation values with a higher level area. The SAE Benchmark is developed to obtain consistent estimation results with a higher level area. This study aims to estimate regional official statistics that are consistent in aggregation to national official statistics when the regional samples is small. In this study, some methods are used, namely Different Benchmark, You-Rao Benchmark, and Augmented Benchmark. These three methods are compared by its consistency, MSE, and RSE. All functions are built in the R software because the package has not yet available for EBLUP Benchmark. In this research, we estimates the School Participation Rates in district level in Indonesia as study case. The data are taken from the 2018 National Socio-Economic Survey (SUSENAS2018) and the 2018 Village Potential Data (PODES2018). Estimation results reveal that the You-Rao Benchmark provides better estimate of School Participation Rates at the national aggregation. A significant contribution of this research is functions in R for EBLUP Benchmarks that can be applied in other official statistics and further research related with benchmarking.

title: Integrated Weighting and Estimation System for Household Surveys with Complex Sampling Design
abstract: The National Institute of Statistic and Census of Argentina (INDEC, in its Spanish acronym) has the task of design, collect and analyse household surveys from which a large part of the indicators produced by the Institute are built. Only during the period 2018-2019, the Permanent Household Survey, the Risk Factor Survey, the Survey of Activities of Children and Teenagers and the Household Expenditure Survey were carried out. The posterior processing and analysis of these surveys after their collection implied the imputation of missing values, adjustment for under-coverage and non-response, calibration of survey weights and the calculation of indicators and their related variance. In this scenario, R results a very powerful and widely used tool in the Institute, which facilitates not only the analysis, but also allow the automation of the step by step process from the reception of the raw data to data delivery and reporting. The INDEC develop several household surveys using probability sampling, where the design includes different levels of stratication, selection with unequal probabilities, several stages of selection, and so on. Therefore, the sampling design is considered complex, what causes that the estimation of variance is not simple. The households are selected from a master sample built after the last 2010 Population Census. A consequence of that is that the selected dwelling may not be found or is no longer used for housing purposes, causing coverage problems. On the other hand, during data collection problems related to non-response cause by absence or refusal of individuals could occur. At the end of the survey, the sample obtained could not represent the major groups of demographic variables such as sex, age or educational level, representing a sub or over representation problem. All the enumerated characteristics and problems are typical on this kind of surveys and there are several solutions in order to decrease the problems they cause. In order to consider the complex sampling design, a bootstrap method developed by Rao and Wu (1988) and Rao, Wu and Yue (1992) is considered. Although the method is developed for multistage stratied sampling with selection with replacement in the rst stage, the non replacement sampling method used in the rst stage of the master sample assures an over estimation of the variance. The coverage and non-response problems are solved using weights adjustment considering different adjustment classes that denes groups of units with the same characteristics. The sub or over representation problem is solved using the calibration of the adjusted sampling weights in order to respect known population totals of demographics variables. All the sampling weights adjustment are applied in each bootstrap replicate to so that they impact the nal estimates. This process is implemented using dierent R packages. This work presents an interactive visual form developed using the R Shiny App that allow the user, even without knowledge in R programming, to dene their own variables and weight adjustment for similar sampling designs and adjustment of weight for coverage, non-response and sub or over representation problems through a user friendly dashboard which can produce results in real time and export them in the required format. This R Shiny App represents an improvement for the INDEC and for any survey statistician in that it allows a faster and more robust sampling weight calculation for it's different surveys.
affiliations: National Institute of Statistics and Censuses; Universidad Nacional de Rosario

title: Calif - shiny application for calibration of weights of statistical surveys
abstract: Statistical Office of the Slovak Republic has performed calibration of survey weights for many years. It has moved from heuristic approaches, across the use of some tailored tools to the own solution. The first version of Calif was made as a Tcl/Tk GUI window back in 2013. This tool enabled users to take advantage of simple environment full of useful statistics that allowed for swift calibration when the most feasible solution was easily found. However, the old-fashioned GUI has found its limits. Therefore, we come with the new interactive web application made in R package shiny that offers very convenient and powerful calibration with many useful outputs and hints, which assist in finding the most feasible calibration trade-off. From the technical point of view, Calif is a shiny navbar page application with many interactive inputs and logical and consistence checks, which makes calibration an intuitive and error resistent process. It is published on GitHub, along with comprehensive documentation.
affiliations: Statistical Office of the Slovak Republic

title: Efficient Autocoding Method in High Dimensional Space
abstract: In recent years, data handled in official statistics is getting more complex and is including high dimensional data. Deep learning methods, SVM, and kernel PCA are commonly used to efficiently classify high dimensional data. The characteristic of these methods is the measurement of the similarity of objects in high dimensional space. On the other hand, we have developed a classification method for autocoding in our previous studies. The developed classifier assigns corresponding classes to target data based on the reliability scores. The previously defined reliability score considers both the uncertainty from data and the uncertainty from the latent classification structure in data. Although the reliability score was defined to correctly classify data that includes uncertainty, it is still difficult to apply this classifier to complex and high dimensional data. The purpose of this study is the development of an efficient autocoding method utilizing metrics in high dimensional space. This study proposes a new method combining the previously developed classifier and metrics in high dimensional space. The proposed method is developed in R utilizing existing R packages for efficient development. We will present our new method for autocoding and the results of classification with governmental survey data during our presentation.
affiliations: National Statistics Center, Japan; University of Tsukuba

title: R script for the development of Cyclic Indicator Systems based on Multivariate Spectral Analysis
abstract: Man has developed diverse methodologies in order to achieve accurate forecasts and, in this way, take advantage of the opportunities that will come to happen or minimize the negative effects of oncoming cataclysms. Cyclic indicator systems are part of this group. Its development originates in the 30s of the last century with the pioneering works of Messrs. Burns and Mitchell, continued by their student Geoffrey Moore. It is they who laid the foundations of indirect forecasting systems for economic phenomena. The first efforts to date ridges and valleys in various time series; to classify them as coincident or leading; and to aggregate them in composite indicators through various coefficient systems, appear in their work. As with a significant number of economic and social applications of the time, common sense predominates in more than one aspect of the numerical procedure. In the absence of adequate computational and analytical tools, they decided to study the relationships between a reference series and only one other series, at a time; and this, based only on some aspects of the behaviour of both series such as ridges and valleys. Therefore, it became of the utmost importance to make a precise dating of both ridges and valleys. Something similar occurred with the determination of weights to form composite indicators. Frequent meetings of experts were frequently held, whose purpose was to determine values for such weights, as well as the replacement of some indicators by others. These meetings were phased out due to the inability to respond to questions such as: how do we determine if changes to the values of the coefficients bring us closer or further from the established purpose? The absence of an optimality criterion to guide these efforts becomes apparent. Despite these limitations, their proposals have been the guideline to follow during the second half of the 20th century. Even today, some international and national organizations continue to look for improvements to update the original proposals. It is our impression that the achievements in this regard have been limited and have incorporated little or nothing of advances that in almost 90 years have taken place in the theory and practice of time series analysis, as well as in the computer systems within our reach today. In this project, we use Fourier analysis in the study of cyclic behaviour of multivariate economic time series taking advantage of advances included in R. The proposal, based on approaches in Brillinger (1981), was originally developed in Fortran77. Using multivariate statistical analysis tools, the cyclic behaviour of vector series using sinusoidal functions seems natural, an approach that has been gaining adherents in various areas of time series economic analysis. The proposed methodology can be summarized as follows: first, indicators close to the notion of principal components (PC) are produced. They allow us to produce versions of the original indicators from which trend has been removed by simply ignoring some low frequencies in the spectral representation of the first PC. These indicators are closer to stationarity, so they can be used to estimate the multivariate pattern of simple and cross covariances. These are in turn used to determine if an indicator “coincides” with, or “leads” the reference one, and by how many periods. In this fashion, groups of coincident and short-, medium- and long-term leading indicators are formed. Each set of these last groups will be used with that of the coincident ones as input to find canonical correlation solutions in the frequency domain. In this way, the values of the coefficients that maximize coherence between the spectral versions of the original indicators without trend or long-term cycles will be determined for each harmonic frequency. Applying the inverse Fourier transform to each solution results in several pairs of composite indicators. Within each of them, the series of indicators show an important correlation for some lag. By construction, the correlation with other couples will, on the other hand, be weak.

title: Business Cycle Tracer of Turkey using R
abstract: The business cycle tracer (BCT) is a visual tool that is used as a means to observe the current state of the economy at a glance. It shows the conjunctural movement of different indicators from various aspects of the economy such as production, consumption, investment, finance, international trade and confidence. In Turkstat, we have been using the BCT system of Statistics Netherlands, which is based on Java and HTML. In the current work flow, we update (monthly) the source data table and the dashboard consisting of charts showing the cyclical movement of 15 indicators along with a short explanation of the current state such as how the indicators are doing in the respective month. This procedure requires a considerable amount of manual work, repeated monthly, and occasionally results in errors due to human mistakes. Starting from 2020 January, we are planning to publish the BCT on the Turkstat website. Therefore, a more automatized / less manual work dependent, more robust and faster standardized approach was required for our purpose. With this aim, an R tool has been developed, which accomplishes the following work flow: - extracting the input data from the source csv files, - temporal disaggregation of the quarterly series based on some regressors, - preparation of a JDemetra+ input, and with that input triggering JDemetra+ cruncher to run a JDemetra+ workspace for outlier adjustment and trend-cycle component extraction, - applying Hodrick-Prescott filter with parameters adjusted for Turkey on the trend-cycle component retrieved by the former step, - standardization and scaling the cycle components of the indicators to fit the BCT, - calculation of the average conjuncture indicator, - drawing the charts and colourization of the background depending on the quadrant of the last observation, - preparation of the dashboard by combining all the charts in one png file, - writing an automatized short explanation mentioning the state of the indicators in the current period and pasting this text in the required field - updating the web site sources by copying and pasting in all the required fields - keeping backup files of each period The only input of the developed R tool is the unadjusted data for the indicators and regressors for the temporal disaggregation (from the web), and the last period of quarterly GDP. Studies on retrieving the raw data within the R script using webservices of the sources are still ongoing. With an end-to-end automatization of the work flow, the monthly update of the BCT will be practical, fast and less prone to errors.

title: IcaRius – A (Not So) Serious Game To Learn R Differently
abstract: Undertaking a review of its information system, the French Institute for Public Statistics (Insee) has selected R and Rstudio IDE as the core of a new range of statistical tools. An ambitious support plan to train Institute staff has been implemented in recent years. Nevertheless, the discovery of R is sometimes hampered by psychological barriers, for part of Insee staff who, accustomed to more closed environments - and therefore more guided tools - see R as a complex programming environment. In order to remove these psychological obstacles, Insee, helped by the community of public statisticians in France and by ThinkR, a consulting and training in R company, is creating a serious game, delivering a new learning experience. This serious game proposes to combine a videogame experience on the one hand, and learning challenges via interactive tutorials in R on the other hand. The world of Statis is indeed threatened by a terrible sorcerer ! The latter seeks to steal the Runes, magic artefacts that allow the people of Statis to live (and count) with confidence. The young icaRius goes on an adventure to save the kingdom, recovering the Runes. IcaRius will have to solve puzzles at key moments in his quest. The answer to these puzzles is found in a grimoire – in which the player progressively discovers the Runes’ language. The Runes’ language is the metaphor used to evoke R in the game. At each puzzle, the grimoire opens a R tutorial, which the trainee must follow and solve to unlock the next part of the game. These tutorials are based on an R-markdown solution, with the learnr and parsons packages (the whole being deployed within a docker image). They allow the trainee to learn R, in a console that hides the technical execution environment. Each tutorial is part of the narrative thread of the game - and allows to keep a strong playful dimension. The icaRius game is developed with the Solarus game engine, an Open Source engine basically dedicated to create replicas of the 1990s Zelda games. Currently under test, the icaRius serious game and its tutorials are intended to be published in open source. Are you ready to help icaRius save the kingdom of Statis? Come discover how one may, while having fun, learn the R language differently - sorry, the Runes’ language !

title: A Reporting And Comparing Application For Province Based Covid-19 Cases In Turkey With R Shiny
abstract: Covid-19 pandemics which emerged in Wuhan, China has been effective still and caused deaths of many people from all over the world. Governments stepped up into a race of taking precautions to prevent the spread of the disease and eventual deaths. Those precautions include partial and whole lockdowns, wearing protective masks in public and shutting down public schools. Turkish government and health ministry in the beginning of the February 2020 announced the normalization of the precautions that they took and started a new procudure of evaluating the risks province- wide. A R-Shiny application is designed to compare weekly announced provincial base number of cases per hundred thousand and to report the differences automatically with interactive graphs and reports. The aim of designing the app is to enable to make comparisons to whole public.

title: Advanced Industrial Turnover Index using Statistical Learning Algorithms
abstract: The modernisation of the production of official statistics should make use not only of new data sources but also of novel statistical methods applied to traditional survey and administrative data. The incorporation of both new data and new methods must improve the traditional quality standards in the production of official statistics. Here we present an application of statistical algorithms to improve the timeliness under a controlled compromise of accuracy of the Spanish Industrial Turnover Index (ITI). We follow the philosophy of the GREG and Sanguiao-Zhang estimators to propose specifically for a cut-off sampling design a combined projective-predictive estimator where already collected data are plugged-in in the estimator whereas not yet collected data are predicted. We use collected values up to time t to train an extreme gradient boosting algorithm on regression trees. We also use both microdata and data collection paradata of the immediately past history of the survey. Preliminary results on data from February 2021 invite us to cherish the hope that the use of these techniques may improve the quality dimension of timeliness while accuracy is kept under controlled. Currently, the survey managers of the Spanish ITI receive three batches for each reference month at days t+20, t+27, t+38 to finally release the first version of the index at t+51. Promising preliminary results are obtained for ITIs for different geographical and economic breakdowns using the preceding estimators trained with the successive batches as well as an initial estimation of the ITI without data of the reference period. Early conclusions from this experimental exercise are: Statistical learning algorithms with high predictive capacity on early data of the reference time period allow us to improve timeliness under a controlled compromise of accuracy; Subject-matter knowledge is crucial for its incorporation into the statistical model, especially on the selection and construction of regressors; Both microdata and paradata are relevant for highquality predicted values; There is still a wide range to further investigate improvements on the predictions both on exploring more algorithms and further complementary data (other surveys, administrative data, and new digital data); Outliers are extremely hard to model and predict and they clearly need management and processing by subject-matter experts.
affiliations: Dept. Methodology and Development of Statistical Production, Statistics Spain; Dept. Statistics and Operations Research, Complutense University of Madrid; S.G. for Industrial and Services Statistics, Statistics Spain

title: Autocoding based on Multi-Class Support Vector Machine by Fuzzy c-means Method
abstract: In recent years, data in official statistics are getting larger and more complex. For developing an autocoding method for the coding task of the Family Income and Expenditure Survey data, which is large and complex data, we have developed the multi-class Support Vector Machine (SVM) by k-means method. In this method, SVM is applied individually to each cluster obtained by k-means method to create the discriminant surface by considering the feature of an individual cluster and obtain a more accurate result for the autocoding. However, since the k-means method is one of the methods of hard clustering in which each data is classified to only one cluster, the k-means method tends to need many clusters to obtain a better solution. In this case, the result has less solution robustness, and a large amount of computation is necessary for obtaining a better solution. To overcome this problem, this study proposes a new classification method based on multi-class SVM that is a combined method of SVM and a fuzzy clustering method. In fuzzy clustering, we can utilize the degree of belongingness of data to clusters and reduce the number of clusters. In this study, we utilize the fuzzy c-means method as the fuzzy clustering method. Several numerical examples show a better performance of the proposed method with the Family Income and Expenditure Survey data.
affiliations: National Statistics Center; Faculty of Engineering, Information and Systems, University of Tsukuba

title: Automating Open Data Publication in Public Health Scotland
abstract: Public Health Scotland (and formerly ISD Scotland) have been publishing open data on the Scottish Health and Social Care Open Data platform since 2017. The platform operates on a CKAN data management system, which has been maintained manually through the web interface by our small open data team up until the end of 2020. With the start of the covid-19 pandemic in 2020, we saw a sudden increase in interest for timely, reliable and well-structured health and social care information. With this sudden growth in both demand and volume of open data to be updated and maintained on the site, our small team had to make some big changes to our upload process to be able to keep up. Updating and replacing 17 files daily and over 500 data files each month manually on the platform had become unmanageable – for both our human team and our technical setup. Initially we developed python code to automate batch uploads of daily covid-19 data – however, we soon shifted to using R instead to align with the skills and experience within our team and support available more widely in our organisation, as well to fit better with our technical infrastructure. Scripts developed in R are scheduled to run on the PHS RStudio Server environment with CRONR, not requiring staff to be logged in or online. Similarly, automated checks are in place to run testing the files match the expected format and in the folders ahead of upload, with automated email notifications flagging up errors or issues that need human response to resolve. Another automated email is sent to confirm successful upload and archival of the daily data files, completing the process without any human interaction required. While this process is functional, we have some future improvements in the pipeline, including more robust error-handling of the pre-upload checks and data delays.

title: Automation forecasting of regional macroeconomic series
abstract: In the same way as many other of agents, economic agents must make decisions in uncertain environments. Since the last crisis and the current pandemic, COVID-19, the number and source of uncertainties have financial-economic increased in magnitude and intensity. Regional agents, closer to the local reality, are looking for both mechanisms capable of showing synthetically the economic situation the regional economy is going through. This paper presents the experience of the Valencian Community (Spain) in the generation of a model of dynamic ensembles of economic forecasts from different organizations implemented in a web application developed with Shiny. The application allows the automation of the annual economic forecasting process, thus facilitating its management by the main economic agents.

title: Building a content delivery pipeline for a website in R
abstract: Statistics Austria (STAT) is currently working towards the release of a new website. An important part of it, namely tables and graphs, will be created using a three step R workflow. 1.The first step of the process is the data import. For the start, two data sources will be supported: STAT’s statistical data base STATcube and the open government data (OGD) portal of STAT, which is also used by other open data portals and therefore this part might especially reusable. The R package STATcubeR handles the data import; It uses a REST API for STATcube and direct CSV downloads for OGD data. 2.The next step is creating the interactive contents: graphs and tables. For that purpose, R packages were developed which utilize the javascript libraries datatable.js and highcharts.js. Both rendering packages use the data format from STATcubeR as an input and create the contents as html-widgets. 3.The last step is to make the content available for the content management system (CMS) where the website articles are written. This is done using a plumber API hosted at rstudio connect. The contents are first created on the R server and saved into a database. The API then accesses the database based on a content-id and returns javascript code for embedding. A graphical user interface was developed to assist non-R users with this process. The GUI was built in shiny and makes it possible to import and edit data to be fit for tabulation or plotting. Afterwards, the user can define customized tables and or graphs using in the GUI. The contents can then be saved and the content id is displayed to the user. The content id can be copy/pasted to the CMS which performs the embedding under the hood. Some of the packages involved in this workflow are available as open source and could be quite useful to other organizations in a similar situation.

title: Computing in the Statistical Office
abstract: Computing with data is at the hart statistical production[1]. Yet, the area of technical computing often falls between the stools of data analysts, IT developers, and methodologists. Typically, data analysts have strong domain knowledge but lack skills in technical computing and software engineering, IT developers have strong software engineering skills but little domain knowledge or knowledge of technical computing. Methodologists frequently have technical computing skills but typically lack strong software development skills. This combination of organizational roles often leads to suboptimal choices when it comes to building (local) statistical production systems. Simply because the necessary skills are not present in a team, or the skills needed are not recognized. This situation is underlined by the lack of attention payed to computing with data in documents such as the Generic Activity Model for Statistical Organizations[2]. In this talk I will analyze the importance of computing with data for activities in the Generic Statistical Business Process Model (GSBPM). Next, I will give a broad overview of skills that are needed to produce statistical output. Finally, I will argue that statistical offices should consider introducing the role of Research Software Engineer (RSE) into their workforce. A RSE combines intimate understanding of data analyses purposes with a solid knowledge of computing with data and software engineering. The current situation is that probably many NSIs have people with an RSE profile in their staff, but they receive no explicit recognition or growth opportunities for their specific set of skills. I therefore also discuss a simple junior/medior/senior model representing growth of RSEs in their role.

title: Dealing with the change of administrative divisions over time
abstract: The administrative divisions of countries change over time. In some countries, some territories change their codes, or names, merge or divide every year. This is the case in France and its communes, counties, regions, departments… As a result, it can be tricky to compare territorial databases from different dates. COGugaison (https://github.com/antuki/COGugaison) is an R package for manipulating French spatial databases produced at different dates by providing the list of existing towns and their history since fifty years and useful functions for transforming databases into geographic codes of other years. The R package CARTElette (https://github.com/antuki/CARTElette) contains geographical layers corresponding to the annual division of the French territories and functions that allow you to load them directly into the {sf} format in R. At this time, those packages only concern France and are therefore only documented in French. Presenting this issue and these packages in this European conference could be a good opportunity to see if (and how) they should be extended to other countries.
affiliations: Ecole nationale d’économie et statistique (ENSAE), France

title: Determinants of house price in Europe
abstract: This paper aims to analyze the determinants of house price in Europe. As independent variables and also as determinants for house prices in Europe we will consider: new constructed dwelling, stock of existing dwelling, households (an indicator of the size of the regional real estate markets), unemployment, purchasing power index (an indicator of purchasing power in different countries), hospitals (a proxy for the quality of available public infrastructure), interest rate, disposable income (a proxy of affordability in housing stock). A panel data for period 2005 – 2019 for European countries will be analyzed using R package ‘plm’. We expect a positive relationship with households, purchasing power index, hospitals, interest rate, disposable income and a negative relationship with new constructed dwelling, stock of existing dwelling and unemployment.
affiliations: Faculty of Business and Administration, University of Bucharest

title: Determining the Business Cycle of Turkey
abstract: In this study, it is aimed to examine the basic characteristics of the cyclical fluctuations in the Turkish economy and to determine the business cycles (contraction and expansion). By using the Bry and Boschan (1971) algorithm, the turning points in the business cycles were obtained. In order to determine the business cycle, Turkey’s monthly Industrial Production Index, monthly and quarterly Gross Domestic Product data were examined and analyzed. As a result of the analysis, the average business cycle for the Turkish economy was calculated as 5 years. It has been observed that this result is compatible with the related studies in the literature and the cycle characteristics of developing countries. Peak and trough points were obtained with the algorithm named “Harding-Pagan (Quarterly Bry-Boschan) Business Cycle Dating Procedure” in the BCDating R package released in 2019. Apart from this, various R packages are used for analysis, visualization and reporting. “dplyr” and “tidyr” were preferred for data manipulation, “ggplot2” and “plotly” for data visualization, and RMarkdown for reporting and presentation.

title: Efficient Computation of approximate Kantorovich-Wasserstein distance for large spatial maps
abstract: In this talk, we present a new R package, called Spatial-KWD and available on the CRAN [1], for the computation of approximate Kantorovich-Wasserstein distance (KWD) between pairs of 2-dimensional distributions defined over a regular grid. KWD is used in various application fields, including image processing and computer science, where it is known with other names, e.g., Earth Mover Distance. In spatial statistics, KWD is a natural choice a measure of (dis-)similarity between spatial maps representing the density of some physical or social quantities, e.g. density of pollutants or density of people, but insofar its adoption has been impeded by the high computational complexity of previous implementations. The computation of the distance (similarity) between two spatial maps can be achieved using the theory of Optimal Transport. The core algorithm of the package implements the Network Simplex algorithm customized for 2-dimensional spatial histograms [2]. The package delivers an approximate solution within a tight deterministic bound. It exposes a tunable parameter to trade-off approximation bound with computation resources (memory, time). Additional features are made available in the package to provide flexibility and adapt to the requirements of different applications. For example, in case of spatial maps with irregular contour, it is possible to compute the KWD over the convex hull or, alternatively, to restrict to geodesic paths within the irregular region. When comparing distributions with different total mass, different options are implemented to deal with the mass. An additional function allows to restrict the computation of the distance within a given focus area embedded in a larger map, so as to measure the local similarity around smaller regions of interest (e.g., a specific urban area within a country). The efficiency of the package is evaluated based on large set of semi-synthetic instances covering the whole Belgium at different grid resolutions. On the larger maps, at resolution of 125m x 125m for a total of 2.5 million of tiles, the package is able to compute the KWD approximation within 1.29% of the exact solution (worst case) in around 10 minutes on a standard desktop computer, while at the resolution of 1km x 1km the resolution completes in around 3.9 seconds within 0.12% of the exact solution. The Spatial-KWD package is the results of a joint collaboration with Eurostat. The source code of the package is freely available online at https://github.com/eurostat/Spatial-KWD. The Spatial-KWD package has been used recently to assess the spatial accuracy of different methods for spatial density estimation of present population based on mobile network operators data [3].
affiliations: University of Pavia, Mathematics Department; Politecnico di Milano, Mathematics Department; European Commission, DG Eurostat, Unit A5, Methodology; Innovation in Official Statistics

title: EMOS coding labs – presentation of preliminary results
abstract: For Eurostat and EMOS community Coding Lab is a way to disseminate outputs that document and share statistical processes beyond just data, but also including code, algorithms, protocols and workflows. In the Statistics Coded users can interactively dialogue with data, explore, reuse and contribute to statistical products. They are distributed in the form of interactive and portable notebooks (in formats such as Jupyter, Rmarkdown and Observable) that combine explanatory text, executable code (in languages such as R, Python and JavaScript), output results and visualisations.

title: Extending data validation with standardised metadata from SDMX registries
abstract: Standardisation of metadata is crucial in official statistics. A harmonized statistical picture of society and economy can only be produced if metadata such as classifications, code lists and variables are agreed among organisations. Internationally these metadata elements are stored in Statistical Data and Metadata Exchange (SDMX) registries. Examples are the Global Registry and the Eurostat Registry. They provide the concepts, variable definitions, data flows, structures and code lists underlying international official statistics. Moreover these registries provide a standardized application programming interface (API) to automatically access specific versions of the metadata from any programming environment. This makes them a key element in international validation processes and hence important for data validation practices in general. The Rpackage validate is a popular tool in official statistics to validate data. Based on a set of predefined validation rules, varying from variable checks to multivariate or statistical checks, the software can execute analyses on possibly large datasets, providing the user with extensive feedback on the health of their data. The software supports the majority of checks that are actually needed in today’s practical International data validation exercises. Validation results are presented graphically and in a machine readable standardized validation report, which can be used as input for consecutive processes. Common rules can be re-used among multiple validation processes. For more details we refer to the online validation cookbook offering recipes for the most common validation scenario’s.
